quote: AP stores settle diverged copies afterwards: last writer wins, vector clocks, or data types that merge by design (CRDTs).
problem: Vector clocks do not settle a conflict. They detect that two versions are concurrent. In Dynamo, versions that cannot be merged automatically are returned to the client, which merges them in application code (the shopping cart union). The list makes vector clocks sound like a resolution rule alongside last-writer-wins and CRDTs.
fix: "AP stores settle diverged copies afterwards: last writer wins, vector clocks that spot the conflict and hand both versions to the application to merge, or data types that merge by design (CRDTs)." Source: DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store", SOSP 2007, §4.4.
reason: Vector clocks detect concurrent versions and do not resolve them. In Dynamo, unmergeable versions go back to the client (DeCandia et al., SOSP 2007, section 4.4). Listing them beside LWW and CRDTs as settling rules is imprecise.
judge_fix: "AP stores settle diverged copies afterwards: last writer wins, vector clocks (which spot the conflict so the application can merge the versions), or data types that merge by design (CRDTs)."

quote: a tight loop that observes the current state of the world, compares it to the desired state

They sleep on a work queue and are woken by watch events from the API server, plus a periodic resync or requeue. The chapter's own code block shows this (RequeueAfter 30 s). A programmer reading "tight loop" will picture continuous polling.
fix: "a loop, woken by every change it watches and by a periodic resync, that observes the current state of the world, compares it to the desired state ..." Source: kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/controller/ (controllers watch the API server); controller-runtime's Reconcile and RequeueAfter.
reason: 'Tight loop' means a busy-polling loop to a programmer (the book itself uses it that way at part-3 line 4894 for event-loop blocking). Controllers wake on watch events plus a timer, as the chapter's own RequeueAfter shows, so the phrase teaches the wrong picture. Findings 9 and 21 are the same.
judge_fix: "is a *reconcile loop*: a short routine, run again on every change it watches and on a timer, that observes the current state of the world, compares it to the desired state, and takes whichever action will move current closer to desired. Run forever."

problem: ch17-containers-p3 closing cause: microVM speed comes mainly from software (a minimal device model and guest kernel), not from hardware virtualization getting cheaper.

problem: ch17-k8s code block and Fig 17.4: the code reads actual state and creates pods through a separate cluster handle (cluster.Get, cluster.Create), and the figure says the controller 'starts one pod'. In Kubernetes, a controller such as the ReplicaSet controller reads and creates Pod objects through the API server, and the kubelet starts the containers. That is what the Fig 17.3 caption itself says ('every component talks only to the API server'), so the code and Fig 17.4 contradict the caption one figure earlier.
reason: Low but real. The code block is labelled 'simplified', but it reads actual state and creates objects through a separate 'cluster' handle one figure after 'every component talks only to the API server'. A one-phrase comment edit removes the apparent contradiction. Leave the Fig 17.4 wording alone, since it describes the loop abstractly.
judge_fix: Code comment: "// 2. observe actual state (from the cluster, also through the API server)".

problem: ch17-k8s-p3, 'a tight loop': Kubernetes controllers are not tight (busy) loops. They wake on watch events and on requeues, with a periodic resync. The code's own RequeueAfter is 30 seconds.
reason: Duplicate of finding 9.
judge_fix: Same as finding 9.

problem: ch17-consensus-p12: 'Real systems escape by ruling out pure asynchrony' is true only of partial synchrony. Ben-Or's randomised protocol runs in a fully asynchronous system and escapes FLP by not being deterministic. Eventual consistency (Dynamo) gives up agreement, not asynchrony. The Fig 17.6 strip frames the three escapes correctly ('Partial synchrony ... randomness ... or weaker agreement'). 'Every working protocol is FLP plus one assumption' is also a stretch for eventual consistency, which does not solve consensus at all.
reason: Internal inconsistency. The lead 'escape by ruling out pure asynchrony' does not fit randomisation (Ben-Or stays asynchronous) or eventual consistency, which the same sentence lists. The Fig 17.6 strip frames the escapes correctly.
judge_fix: Replace "Real systems escape by ruling out pure asynchrony:" with "Real systems escape by relaxing one of its conditions:". Keep the three examples and the closing line.

problem: SolarWinds, inconsistent across chapters: ch15-defense-p6 says the attackers 'modified the source code of its Orion ... product', while ch17-microservices-p7 says the update was 'poisoned at build-time inside SolarWinds's own build system'. p7 is the accurate one: the SUNSPOT implant swapped in a backdoored source file only while the build ran and then restored the original (CrowdStrike, 'SUNSPOT: An Implant in the Build Process', Jan 2021), so the stored source was clean. Read together, ch15's wording undercuts p7's point that reproducible builds (rebuild from source, compare) are the answer. Low severity. Reconcile ch15-defense-p6 to 'swapped a source file during the build'.
reason: Real cross-chapter inconsistency, located in public/part-4.html line 3318 (ch15 SolarWinds callout), not in ch17. ch15 says the attackers 'modified the source code of its Orion product', while ch17 (correctly) says it was poisoned at build time. Per CrowdStrike's SUNSPOT analysis (Jan 2021), the implant swapped a backdoored file in during the build and restored the original, so the stored source stayed clean. Left as is, ch15 undercuts the reproducible-builds defence that both chapters cite. Low severity.
judge_fix: In ch15, replace "modified the source code of its Orion network monitoring product to insert a backdoor (called SUNBURST)" with "swapped a backdoored source file into each build of its Orion network monitoring product, then restored the original so the stored source stayed clean (the backdoor is called SUNBURST)".

problem: The paragraph's last sentence repeats, almost word for word, the clause just before it ('Argo CD and Flux run it as a loop, while Terraform and Pulumi run it only when a person asks...'). It looks like an editing slip. The Fig 17.4 strip ('Elsewhere') then says the same thing a third time.

Keep its one new detail in p3: 'Argo CD and Flux run it as a loop over a Git repository, while Terraform and Pulumi run it only when a person asks, working out the changes needed (the plan) and applying them once.' quote: takes whichever action will move current closer to desired. Run forever.
problem: 'Run forever.' is a clipped dramatic fragment. 'A tight loop' also contradicts the code block just below, where a converged controller asks to run again after 30 seconds ('RequeueAfter: 30 * time.Second'). A controller does not spin.

quote: Idempotent. A pass with nothing to fix changes nothing, so running the loop often is safe.
problem: The strip's 'Level, not edge' and 'Idempotent' bullets repeat what ch17-k8s-p3 has just said (idempotent, robust, stateless). In p3 that sentence is also a reflexive triplet with the same opening three times ('The loop is idempotent... The loop is robust... The loop is stateless').

Cut the strip bullets 'Level, not edge' and 'Idempotent'. If the strip needs content, add the one new fact: 'Requeue. A controller with nothing to do asks to run again later (30 seconds in the code below), so drift is caught even when no event arrives.'
reason: All three Fig 17.4 strip bullets restate p3 (level-triggered = stateless/robust, idempotent, elsewhere). The strip as written holds no new fact. The p3 prose triplet is parallel on purpose and each member is explained, so leave p3's sentences alone (reject that part of the proposed fix).
judge_fix: Strip: keep 'Level, not edge' (it names the term of art), cut 'Idempotent.' (and 'Elsewhere', see n1), and add one new fact that the code block only implies: '*Requeue.* A controller with nothing to do asks to run again later (30 seconds in the code below), so drift is caught even when no event arrives.'

quote: a container starts in milliseconds, weighs a few megabytes, and shares the host's kernel
problem: The start-time numbers disagree. The same paragraph says 'docker run nginx'... 'the whole thing takes a second' and calls it 'a tenfold to hundredfold improvement' over a VM's 'tens of seconds'. That ratio fits one second, not milliseconds. In ch17-containers-p3, microVMs boot 'in about a tenth of a second' while 'preserving most of containers' speed'. That claim fails if a container starts in milliseconds, and it reverses if a container takes a second.
fix: '...a container starts in under a second, weighs a few megabytes, and shares the host's kernel.' Then: 'Once the image is downloaded, `docker run nginx` creates the namespaces, configures cgroups, and starts the process in about a second.'
reason: Numbers disagree: 'milliseconds' vs 'the whole thing takes a second' (which also includes the download) vs the 10x-100x ratio against tens of seconds, vs the microVM claim of 'about a tenth of a second ... preserving most of containers' speed', which would make the microVM faster than the container. Ch4's Fig 4.19 says a container 'starts like a process'.
judge_fix: containers-p1: 'a container starts in a fraction of a second, weighs a few megabytes, and shares the host's kernel.' and 'Running `docker run nginx` ... starts the process; once the image is on the machine, that takes well under a second.' Keep 'tenfold to hundredfold'. In containers-p3 write 'boot in about an eighth of a second' (Firecracker's ~125 ms, as ch4 says) and 'near-VM isolation at close to container speed and density'.

quote: any two quorums must intersect in at least one node
problem: The chapter explains majority overlap three times. ch17-consensus-p2 says 'any two of them share at least one acceptor', p6 says it again, and the Fig 17.5 strip says 'Any two majorities of the same cluster share a node... N nodes tolerate ⌊(N − 1)/2⌋ failures, which is why clusters run 3, 5 or 7'. The strip also repeats p4/p6's N = 2f + 1 and the point about cluster sizes. 'Quorum' is defined twice too: 'a quorum (a majority)' in p2 and again, in bold as if new, in p4.

Cut the strip's 'Majorities' bullet to 'In log replication an entry counts once a majority hold it, so any later leader's majority includes a node that has it.'
reason: The majority-overlap idea is stated in p2, p6 and the Fig 17.5 strip, and the strip also repeats p4/p6's N = 2f+1 and 3/5/7 point. 'quorum (a majority)' in p2 also uses the term before the callout defines it. The p6 rewrite is optional; the strip cut and the p2 change are what matter.
judge_fix: p2: replace 'to a quorum (a majority) of acceptors' with 'to a majority of acceptors'. Strip 'Majorities' bullet: '*Majorities.* In **log replication** an entry counts once a majority hold it, so any later leader's majority includes a node that has it and a committed entry is never lost.' Leave p6 as it is.

quote: Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout published Raft in 2014 as an understandable alternative to Paxos
problem: The reader is told three times that Raft is the understandable alternative to Paxos: ch17-consensus-p1 ('Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout's Raft (2014), which was explicitly designed to be more understandable than Paxos'), p2 ('a complete design built to be understood') and this strip bullet.

reason: Authors, year and 'understandable alternative to Paxos' are already in p1 and p2 (and the glossary). The strip bullet repeats them.

quote: in a fully asynchronous system with even one crash, no deterministic protocol is guaranteed both to agree and to finish
problem: FLP is stated four times in one section: ch17-consensus-p8, the Fig 17.6 caption, this strip ('The theorem'), and the math callout p11. The strip's 'The escapes' bullet then gives the same three escapes, with the same examples (Paxos/Raft, Ben-Or, Dynamo), as p12.
fix: Cut the strip bullets 'The theorem' and 'The escapes' and keep only 'In practice', which is new. The callout (p10–p12) then gives the formal statement and the escapes once.
reason: FLP is stated in p8, the Fig 17.6 caption, the strip 'The theorem', and the callout p11; the strip 'The escapes' repeats the callout's p12 list with the same examples. Only 'In practice' is new.
judge_fix: Fig 17.6 strip: delete 'The theorem' and 'The escapes'; keep only '*In practice.* Raft never decides wrongly, but during a long network storm it can stall, electing leader after leader until messages arrive in time again.' If wanted, move the phrase 'safe always, live once delays settle' into p12's partial-synchrony clause.

quote: Real systems escape by ruling out pure asynchrony
problem: Only the first of the three escapes listed rules out asynchrony. Randomisation (Ben-Or) works in a fully asynchronous system by giving up determinism. Eventual consistency weakens agreement. So the sentence contradicts its own list, and it contradicts p8's framing that each escape adds an assumption.
fix: 'Real systems escape by dropping one of the theorem's conditions: partial synchrony (Paxos, Raft) assumes messages eventually arrive within some bound; randomisation (Ben-Or) gives up determinism and flips coins to break adversarial schedules; eventual consistency (Dynamo) weakens agreement, serving now and reconciling later.'
reason: Only partial synchrony rules out pure asynchrony. Ben-Or randomisation works in a fully asynchronous system by giving up determinism, and eventual consistency weakens agreement. The sentence contradicts its own list and the theorem's stated conditions (asynchronous, deterministic, agreement).
judge_fix: p12: 'Real systems escape by dropping one of the theorem's conditions: _partial synchrony_ (Paxos, Raft) assumes messages eventually arrive within some bound; _randomisation_ (Ben-Or) gives up determinism and flips coins to break adversarial schedules; _eventual consistency_ (Dynamo) weakens agreement, serving now and reconciling later.'

quote: Every working protocol is FLP plus one assumption.

reason: 'Every working protocol is FLP plus one assumption' restates p8's closer ('works around FLP by adding an assumption, and the assumption is the price') and ends the section on an aphorism.

quote: Why? Because the moment you need multiple machines to agree on something
problem: A rhetorical question stands in for a plain causal clause. It is followed by three clipped sentences in a row ('Messages can be delayed arbitrarily. Machines can crash. The network can partition...'), the clipped-fragment pattern the brief names.
fix: 'Kubernetes' "source of truth", etcd, runs a distributed consensus protocol called Raft, because the moment you need multiple machines to agree on something (...), the network's unreliability becomes a mathematical problem: messages can be delayed arbitrarily, machines can crash, and the network can partition into halves that can't reach each other.'
reason: 'Why? Because' is filler wrapped around a plain causal clause, followed by three short sentences that read as a list pattern. Cheap to repair, and the owner's law 2 targets exactly this.
judge_fix: 'Kubernetes' "source of truth", etcd, runs a distributed consensus protocol called *Raft*, because the moment you need multiple machines to agree on something (what is the current version of the configuration, who is the current leader, what is the next entry in the log), the network's unreliability becomes a mathematical problem. Messages can be delayed arbitrarily, machines can crash, and the network can partition into halves that can't reach each other.'

quote: Availability (every request gets a response)
problem: By this definition the CP replica in Fig 17.7 is still available, because 'error: can't confirm' is a response. A careful reader stops when the figure calls an error-returning system 'unavailable'. Brewer's and Gilbert–Lynch's sense is a non-error answer.
fix: '*Availability* (every request gets a real answer, not an error)'
reason: As written, the CP replica's 'error: can't confirm' is a response, so the figure's 'unavailable' contradicts the definition. The standard formal sense (Gilbert and Lynch; Brewer's follow-up) is a non-error answer from a non-failing node. Wikipedia's CAP article states 'non-error response'.
judge_fix: '*Availability* (every request gets a real answer, not an error)'

'Why not CA' repeats 'Network partitions happen whether you like it or not'. The caption restates p1's last two sentences (refuse and lose A, or serve stale and lose C).

quote: Containers abstract operating systems but preserve the cost of process isolation.

quote: SBOMs (software bills of materials, a list of every component inside a program), reproducible builds
problem: Chapter 15 §05 (ch15-defense, 'SolarWinds 2020 · the supply-chain shape') already tells this story: the build compromise, the signed update, ~18,000 customers, and the same three responses (SBOMs, reproducible builds, signed build provenance).
